title: Developmental Disabilities — Causes, Prevention & Early Identification (Set 7)
subtitle: Genetic, prenatal, perinatal & postnatal causes; Down syndrome, Fragile X, FASD & PKU; prevention, newborn screening & early intervention
scenario: Understanding, at an introductory level, the possible causes of developmental disabilities—genetic, prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal—along with prevention, newborn screening, early identification, and a respectful, non-blaming approach to the person.

steps.q: The possible causes of developmental disabilities are often grouped by WHEN they occur. These groupings include:

opts.text: Genetic causes and causes occurring before birth (prenatal), around birth (perinatal), and after birth (postnatal)—with many cases of unknown cause
opts.rat: Causes are commonly organized as genetic/chromosomal and by timing—prenatal (before birth), perinatal (around the time of birth), and postnatal (after birth)—and in many individuals the exact cause is unknown.

opts.text: Only causes that happen in adulthood
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities originate during the developmental period (before adulthood), not solely in adulthood.

opts.text: Only contagious infections passed between clients
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are not caught from other clients; causes are varied and not contagious.

opts.text: Only the client's own choices
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are not caused by the client's choices.

steps.q: Down syndrome is caused by:

opts.text: Something the child ate after birth
opts.rat: Down syndrome is a chromosomal condition present from conception, not caused by diet after birth.

opts.text: An extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21)
opts.rat: Down syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), a chromosomal difference present from conception. (Confirm genetics wording with faculty.)

opts.text: A contagious virus spread in group homes
opts.rat: Down syndrome is genetic/chromosomal and is not contagious.

opts.text: Poor parenting after birth
opts.rat: Down syndrome is not caused by parenting; it is a chromosomal condition.

steps.q: Fragile X syndrome is best described as:

opts.text: An injury that happens during childhood play
opts.rat: Fragile X is a genetic condition, not an injury.

opts.text: A condition caused by prenatal alcohol
opts.rat: Alcohol-related effects are FASD; Fragile X is an inherited genetic condition.

opts.text: An inherited (genetic) condition and a recognized genetic cause of intellectual disability
opts.rat: Fragile X syndrome is an inherited genetic condition and a recognized genetic cause of intellectual disability. (Confirm specifics with faculty.)

opts.text: A contagious illness
opts.rat: Fragile X is genetic and inherited, not contagious.

steps.q: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is caused by:

opts.text: A chromosome the child inherits
opts.rat: FASD is not inherited through chromosomes; it results from prenatal alcohol exposure.

opts.text: An infection caught after birth
opts.rat: FASD is caused before birth by alcohol exposure, not by a postnatal infection.

opts.text: A head injury in adulthood
opts.rat: FASD originates from prenatal alcohol exposure, not an adult injury.

opts.text: The mother's alcohol use during pregnancy, and it is preventable
opts.rat: FASD results from alcohol crossing the placenta during pregnancy and affecting fetal development. Because the cause is prenatal alcohol exposure, it is preventable.

steps.q: Because FASD is caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, the most effective prevention is:

opts.text: Avoiding alcohol entirely during pregnancy
opts.rat: Since there is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy, avoiding alcohol entirely during pregnancy is the way to prevent FASD.

opts.text: Taking extra vitamins after the baby is born
opts.rat: Postnatal vitamins do not prevent a condition caused by prenatal alcohol exposure.

opts.text: Special schooling in later childhood
opts.rat: Education supports the child but does not prevent FASD, which is determined before birth.

opts.text: Genetic testing of the parents
opts.rat: FASD is not inherited, so genetic testing does not prevent it; avoiding prenatal alcohol does.

steps.q: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is:

opts.text: A contagious childhood infection
opts.rat: PKU is an inherited metabolic condition, not a contagious infection.

opts.text: An inherited metabolic condition that is detected by newborn screening and managed with a special diet
opts.rat: PKU is an inherited disorder of metabolism identified through newborn screening; early dietary management (limiting phenylalanine) helps prevent intellectual disability. (Confirm dietary/medical details with faculty.)

opts.text: Caused only by a birth injury
opts.rat: PKU is inherited and metabolic, not caused by birth injury.

opts.text: A condition with no available treatment
opts.rat: PKU is managed, notably through early dietary treatment, when detected early.

steps.q: Newborn screening programs are valuable because they:

opts.text: Replace the need for any later health care
opts.rat: Screening is an early step; it does not replace ongoing health care.

opts.text: Are only paperwork with no health benefit
opts.rat: Newborn screening detects treatable conditions and has clear health benefits.

opts.text: Detect certain conditions early so treatment can begin before serious harm occurs
opts.rat: Newborn screening can identify conditions such as PKU early, allowing treatment to start promptly and prevent or reduce harm.

opts.text: Diagnose conditions that appear only in adulthood
opts.rat: Newborn screening targets conditions detectable at birth, not adult-onset conditions.

steps.q: Which is an example of a PRENATAL cause (occurring before birth) of a developmental disability?

opts.text: A fall on the playground at age eight
opts.rat: An injury at age eight is a postnatal event, not prenatal.

opts.text: A brain infection contracted as a toddler
opts.rat: An infection during toddlerhood is postnatal, not prenatal.

opts.text: Lack of oxygen during a difficult delivery
opts.rat: Oxygen loss during delivery is a perinatal (around-birth) cause, not prenatal.

opts.text: A maternal infection during pregnancy (such as rubella) or exposure to alcohol, drugs, or toxins
opts.rat: Prenatal causes occur before birth—examples include certain maternal infections during pregnancy (such as rubella), poor prenatal nutrition, and exposure to alcohol, drugs, or toxins. (Confirm specific examples with faculty.)

steps.q: Which is an example of a PERINATAL cause (occurring around the time of birth)?

opts.text: Oxygen deprivation during a difficult birth, or complications of prematurity
opts.rat: Perinatal causes happen around the time of birth—examples include lack of oxygen (birth complications) and problems related to prematurity or very low birth weight.

opts.text: An inherited chromosome difference present from conception
opts.rat: An inherited chromosomal difference is a genetic cause, not a perinatal event.

opts.text: Lead poisoning during the preschool years
opts.rat: Lead poisoning in the preschool years is a postnatal cause.

opts.text: A car accident in adolescence
opts.rat: An injury in adolescence is a postnatal cause, not perinatal.

steps.q: Which is an example of a POSTNATAL cause (occurring after birth)?

opts.text: An extra chromosome present at conception
opts.rat: A chromosomal difference at conception is genetic, not postnatal.

opts.text: A brain infection (such as meningitis or encephalitis), a head injury, or lead poisoning in childhood
opts.rat: Postnatal causes occur after birth—examples include brain infections (meningitis, encephalitis), serious head injury, near-drowning, and lead poisoning during childhood.

opts.text: Alcohol exposure before birth
opts.rat: Prenatal alcohol exposure is a prenatal cause, not postnatal.

opts.text: A complication that happened during delivery
opts.rat: A delivery complication is a perinatal cause, not postnatal.

steps.q: One way to help prevent developmental disability from lead poisoning in children is to:

opts.text: Encourage children to play with old painted items
opts.rat: Old paint can contain lead; encouraging contact would increase risk.

opts.text: Ignore possible sources of lead exposure
opts.rat: Ignoring lead sources increases the risk of poisoning.

opts.text: Reduce children's exposure to lead sources, such as old lead-based paint or contaminated water
opts.rat: Lead exposure can damage the developing brain; reducing exposure to sources like old lead-based paint and contaminated water helps prevent lead poisoning. (Confirm current guidance with faculty.)

opts.text: Treat lead poisoning only after severe symptoms appear
opts.rat: Prevention and early detection are key; waiting for severe symptoms risks lasting harm.

steps.q: Taking folic acid before and during early pregnancy is recommended because it helps prevent:

opts.text: All developmental disabilities of every kind
opts.rat: Folic acid reduces the risk of specific birth defects; it does not prevent all developmental disabilities.

opts.text: Injuries that happen during adolescence
opts.rat: Folic acid relates to early fetal development, not adolescent injuries.

opts.text: Contagious childhood infections
opts.rat: Folic acid does not prevent infections; immunizations and hygiene address those.

opts.text: Certain birth defects of the brain and spine (neural tube defects)
opts.rat: Adequate folic acid before and during early pregnancy helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects—birth defects of the brain and spine. (Confirm current recommendations with faculty.)

steps.q: Good prenatal care (regular checkups, proper nutrition, and avoiding harmful substances) is important because it:

opts.text: Helps reduce the risk of some developmental disabilities and supports healthy fetal development
opts.rat: Prenatal care—checkups, nutrition, and avoiding alcohol, drugs, tobacco, and other harmful exposures—supports healthy development and lowers the risk of some developmental disabilities.

opts.text: Guarantees that no disability can ever occur
opts.rat: Prenatal care reduces risk but cannot guarantee prevention; many causes are not preventable.

opts.text: Has no effect on the developing baby
opts.rat: Prenatal care clearly affects fetal health and development.

opts.text: Is only needed after the baby is born
opts.rat: Prenatal care occurs during pregnancy; care after birth is separate and also important.

steps.q: Immunizations (such as protection against rubella and measles) help prevent developmental disability by:

opts.text: Curing conditions that are already present at birth
opts.rat: Immunizations prevent infections; they do not cure conditions already present.

opts.text: Preventing certain infections that can damage the developing brain
opts.rat: Some infections (such as rubella in pregnancy or measles complications) can harm brain development; immunization helps prevent these infections and their consequences. (Confirm specifics with faculty.)

opts.text: Replacing the need for prenatal care
opts.rat: Immunizations complement—not replace—prenatal and general health care.

opts.text: Working only after a disability has developed
opts.rat: Immunizations are preventive, given to avoid infection before it occurs.

steps.q: In many individuals with a developmental disability, the exact cause:

opts.text: Is always clearly known
opts.rat: The cause is not always identifiable; it is unknown in many cases.

opts.text: Is always the parents' fault
opts.rat: Blaming parents is inaccurate; many causes are not preventable or identifiable.

opts.text: Is unknown or cannot be identified
opts.rat: Despite advances, the specific cause of a developmental disability is unknown in a substantial number of individuals.

opts.text: Is always a contagious infection
opts.rat: Causes are varied and often non-infectious; developmental disabilities are not contagious.

steps.q: Which statement about developmental disabilities is TRUE?

opts.text: They can be caught from another person like a cold
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are not contagious.

opts.text: They are caused by something the client did wrong
opts.rat: They are not the result of the client's actions or choices.

opts.text: They only appear for the first time in adulthood
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities originate during the developmental period, not first in adulthood.

opts.text: They are not contagious and are not caused by anything the client 'did wrong'
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are not contagious and are not the client's fault; they arise from genetic, prenatal, perinatal, or postnatal factors, many outside anyone's control.

steps.q: Genetic counseling can help families primarily by:

opts.text: Providing information about inherited conditions and possible risks so families can make informed decisions
opts.rat: Genetic counseling gives families information about inherited conditions, patterns, and risks, supporting informed decision-making and planning.

opts.text: Guaranteeing that no child will ever have a disability
opts.rat: Counseling informs about risk; it cannot guarantee outcomes.

opts.text: Blaming a parent for a child's condition
opts.rat: Genetic counseling is informational and supportive, not a way to assign blame.

opts.text: Replacing the child's need for services
opts.rat: Counseling supports the family's understanding; it does not replace the child's services.

steps.q: Early identification and early intervention (starting services when a child is young) are important because:

opts.text: They are only about paperwork and funding
opts.rat: Early intervention has real developmental benefits, not just administrative ones.

opts.text: Starting supports early can improve a child's development, skills, and long-term outcomes
opts.rat: Identifying delays early and beginning intervention promptly can strengthen development, build skills, and improve long-term outcomes for the child and family.

opts.text: They should wait until the child is an adult
opts.rat: The value of early intervention is that it begins early, not in adulthood.

opts.text: They remove the need for any family involvement
opts.rat: Family involvement is central to early intervention, not removed by it.

steps.q: Understanding the cause of a client's developmental disability is most useful because it can:

opts.text: Show who is to blame for the disability
opts.rat: The purpose is care and support, not assigning blame.

opts.text: Justify treating the client differently or unfairly
opts.rat: Knowing a cause never justifies unfair treatment; all clients deserve respectful care.

opts.text: Help guide health monitoring and individualized care, since some conditions have associated health needs
opts.rat: Some conditions carry known associated health needs, so understanding the cause can help guide appropriate health monitoring and individualized care and services.

opts.text: Prove the disability is contagious
opts.rat: Developmental disabilities are not contagious; identifying a cause does not change that.

steps.q: Regardless of the cause of a client's developmental disability, the technician's approach should be to:

opts.text: Focus on assigning blame for the condition
opts.rat: Blame has no place in respectful, person-centered care.

opts.text: Treat the client differently based on their diagnosis label
opts.rat: Care is based on the individual's needs and strengths, not on labels.

opts.text: Limit the client's opportunities because of their cause
opts.rat: Care supports opportunity and participation, not limitation.

opts.text: Treat the client with respect and focus on their individual needs, strengths, and supports
opts.rat: Whatever the cause, each client deserves respectful, person-centered care focused on their individual needs, strengths, and the supports that help them thrive.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Developmental Disabilities. Written at an introductory level from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Genetic and medical etiology facts (chromosomal basis of Down syndrome, Fragile X, PKU and its dietary management, folic acid and neural-tube-defect prevention, congenital rubella, lead-exposure guidance, and immunization) are stated at an introductory level and marked for faculty confirmation. No statistics or prevalence figures are asserted. Pending faculty review.
